flashcards.q: Map the four 2026 API protocol choices to their non-overlapping niches: REST, GraphQL, gRPC, tRPC.
flashcards.a: REST = public APIs (CDN caching, debuggability). GraphQL = aggregation layer serving diverse client shapes from one backend. gRPC = internal service-to-service (binary, HTTP/2, auto deadline propagation). tRPC = TypeScript full-stack, same team owns both ends, eliminates the API boundary's type gap entirely.

flashcards.q: List the four Richardson Maturity Model levels, and where most production APIs deliberately stop.
flashcards.a: L0 swamp of POX (one endpoint, everything's POST), L1 real resource URLs, L2 correct HTTP verbs + status codes, L3 HATEOAS (hypermedia links). Most production APIs deliberately stop at L2 -- L3's dynamic-discovery benefit rarely justifies its cost for a typical hardcoded-client population.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, why does offset pagination degrade at scale while cursor pagination doesn't?
flashcards.a: OFFSET N forces the database to scan and discard N rows every time -- not index-friendly, cost grows linearly with depth. Cursor pagination (WHERE col > :last ORDER BY col LIMIT N) is a real indexable predicate -- the database seeks directly via the index, cost stays roughly constant at any depth.

flashcards.q: What does cursor pagination give up that offset pagination provides?
flashcards.a: The ability to jump to an arbitrary page number, or cheaply show a total page count -- cursor pagination is inherently sequential, only movable forward/backward from a known position.

flashcards.q: What are RFC 9457's five standard Problem Details members, and what RFC did it supersede?
flashcards.a: type, title, status, detail, instance (plus arbitrary extension fields). Supersedes RFC 7807 (2016) as of August 2023 -- both describe compatible shapes, tooling generally targets either interchangeably.

flashcards.q: What percentage of real-time use cases does SSE cover, and what's SSE's built-in reconnection mechanism?
flashcards.a: ~95%. Built-in reconnection via the Last-Event-ID header -- the browser's EventSource automatically reconnects on disconnect and sends the last event id it received, letting the server resume the stream rather than replay from the start.

flashcards.q: Name the genuine 5% use cases that justify WebSocket over SSE.
flashcards.a: Cases needing genuine bidirectional, low-latency, binary-capable communication: voice/video signaling, collaborative multi-cursor editing, gaming input streams -- not general 'real-time' needs, which SSE covers.

flashcards.q: What's the specific caching bug header-based API versioning is prone to, and how is it avoided?
flashcards.a: A CDN/cache keying purely on URL serves a cached v1 response to a v2 request hitting the same URL, unless the server correctly sets Vary: Accept (or equivalent) at EVERY layer in the caching chain. URL-path versioning avoids this class of bug entirely by construction, since each version has a genuinely distinct URL.

flashcards.q: Which real companies use date-based API versioning, and what workload does it suit?
flashcards.a: Stripe and GitHub. Suits platforms shipping frequent, fine-grained breaking changes -- clients pin to a specific date/snapshot rather than forcing every small change through a new major URL-path version.

flashcards.q: What GraphQL mechanism lets a partial response succeed even when one underlying service fails, and why is this a genuine advantage over a typical REST aggregation endpoint?
flashcards.a: GraphQL returns successfully-resolved fields alongside a structured error entry (in the errors array, associated with the failed field's path) for the fields that failed, rather than failing the entire query -- a REST aggregation endpoint more commonly succeeds or fails as one atomic unit.

flashcards.q: What's tRPC's core value proposition, and what's its real limitation?
flashcards.a: Eliminates the API contract boundary for a TypeScript full-stack app -- backend function signatures ARE the contract, imported directly with full type inference, no schema/codegen, no contract-drift bugs. Limitation: requires both ends to be TypeScript in the same monorepo/type-sharing pipeline -- no benefit for external partners or non-TypeScript consumers.

flashcards.q: Should every POST endpoint accept an idempotency key?
flashcards.a: No -- only endpoints with real, costly-to-duplicate side effects (payments, provisioning, notifications). A naturally-idempotent-by-construction endpoint (e.g. an upsert keyed on a client-provided ID) or a purely read-adjacent one doesn't need the extra mechanism.
